I've read the book 'Scarlett' and was expecting a good movie the first time I saw it. I'm afraid to say that I was disappointed. The movie did not follow the book and made many changes that I did not like. One of the changes that I did not like the way that Lord Fenton was portrayed. It made no sense to make him out to be a bad man. The way that things ended between Lord Fenton and Scarlett was a lot different and their whole relationship was too intimate. There was also a lot less confrontation between Scarlett and Rhett in the movie than was originally written in the book. The movie sent the two in two completely opposite ways and they did not seem to cross paths often enough to make it seem like there still could be love between the two. I recently watched the movie 'The Notebook' and was happy to say that I really enjoyed most of it. However, I must say that I was disappointed that the movie deviated from the book and made some changes that I did not like. Out of all of the changes, I did not like the way that Lord Fenton was portrayed. It made no sense that he turned out to be a married man. The way that things ended with Lord Fenton in the book was a lot different and a whole lot more... intimate. There was also a lot less interaction between Scarlett and Rhett in the movie than was originally written in the book. The movie sent the two in almost completely different directions and they did not seem to cross paths often enough to show the kind of chemistry that could have developed between the two. A good movie, but I think that the movie could have been better than it was, had it stayed true to Anne Rippley's book.

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a failed Swedish book editor who decides to take a non-stop train to Berlin. Unfortunately for everyone around him, he's a walking disaster, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. The train also holds a man and his mistress scheming to murder the man's wife (who's also on the train), a soldier on his way home, two gay elderly gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two nuns, a bunch of refugees, and even more people. Meant as a mix of noir-ish thriller (which it does quite well - at least to begin with), and comedy, the film fails with both. It doesn't sit right as the film changes tone with every new scene. And as the train races towards its final destination, the film turns more and more bizarre, ending on a truly surreal note. The good bits are wasted in a myriad of pointless plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small the part is. It feels like the filmmakers rang everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Too bad that the performances are just as bad as the script (act your lines - don't read them!). The comedy is more or less slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pace is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually) with on scene in particular dragging on for about ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to think that swearing is a good way to replace decent dialogue. The film looks great though, in moody B&W, but it's wasted on such inept film-making in every other department. [1/10]

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a failed Swedish book editor who finds himself on a non-stop train to Berlin. Unknown to everyone around him, he's a walking bomb, causing mayhem everywhere he goes. The train also holds a man and his mistress scheming to murder the doctor's wife (who is also on the train), a soldier on his way to the front, a young woman on the train to escape a jealous lover, a group of refugees, and many more. Positioning itself as a mix of a noist thriller (which it seems to be - at least to begin with) and comedy, the film fails at both. It doesn't help help that the film changes tone with every new scene. Even as the train races towards its final destination, the film becomes more and more serious, ending on a very depressing note. The funny bits are buried in a myriad of pointless plots and characters. Skenbart is packed with famous Swedish actors, but not one plays the part well. It's like the filmmakers called everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part. The script is incredibly bad, and the actors who are bad as the script overact to lines that don't read well. The comedy is more or less slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pacing is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually) - one scene in particular goes on for about ten minutes for no good reason. Skenbart also seems to think that silence is a good way to replace decent dialogue. The film looks good, shot in moody B&W, but it's built on such shoddy film-making in in every department. [1]/10

It devours anything that happens upon it by absorbing and then dissolving it in what appears to be orange Fanta. There is an artist who fell victim to the bed, but was sick and ends up behind a painting in the room it inhabits. The narrative is told entirely through him. This movie fails horribly at everything, even at being bad. Still, it's not without its own brand of charm.

I, like most other people, saw this movie after hearing of it from Patton Oswalt. Oddly enough, it was easier to watch than I thought it would be. However, it shouldn't come as a surprise that I was not used. The plot is very simple and is contained within the title. It is a bed of nails. Nothing more, nothing less. There is an effort to throw in a story, but not much of it happens. A snake has somehow ended up in the bed and, as a result, it is hungry. It devours anything that happens upon it. There is a man who is in search of a can of Fanta. There is an artist who is trying to find where the bed was hidden and ends up behind a painting in the room it inhabits. The narrative is told entirely through dialogue. This movie fails horribly as entertainment, even as a comedy. Still, it's not without its own brand of entertainment

For me Hurt is Crisp and I've always found it very hard to take the man himself because Hurt was more him than he was himself. Its masterful performance. Quentin the man is always interesting, but his life as portrayed is really not. I am disappointed by the film. I've always admired the man and his unique point of view. I just wish he was better served by this film about his life.

Trite and unoriginal. It's like someone watched Immortal Beloved and Amadeus and decided to mix them together and, in the process, steal other formulaic plot parts from other movies to make another one. As with most historical movies nowadays, there are some inaccuracies as history is manipulated to better suit the story, which is understandable for the most part. For example, during the remaining days of Beethoven's life, it was necessary for other people to write down what they needed to say in order for him to understand them. That, of course, would have been a nuisance to have to show on screen. The script, although filled with some quotable lines, doesn't quite capture the feel of that time period and, coupled with some bad acting, seems rather contemporary. Diane Kruger is nice enough to look at but she still has lots to improve on her craft. Ed Harris doesn't work for me as Beethoven and I mostly blame Gary Oldman for that. Overall, not a very good interpretation of the musical maestro's life. Better just find yourself a copy of Immortal Beloved. http://iwascalledclementine.multiply.com/reviews

Trite and unoriginal. It's like someone watched Immortal Beloved Woman a few times and decided to copy it, and then they went on to steal other formulaic plot parts from other movies. That's one big problem with so many movies nowadays. There are some parts where history is altered to fit into the movie, but it works for the most part. For example, in the early days of Shakespeare's life, he didn't need other people to write down what they needed to say in order for him to repeat them. That, I imagine, would have been a nuisance to whoever was performing on stage. The score, although it has some good orchestr moments, doesn't quite capture the feel of that time period and, coupled with the special effects, seems rather dated. Diane Kruger is always good to look at and she certainly has lots of scenes in this movie. Ed Harris doesn't work for me as a character and I blame Gary Oldman for that. Overall, not a very good adaptation of a classic that was a play. Better just find yourself a copy of Immortal Beloved Woman. http://iwascalledclementine.multiply.com/reviews

Of all of the post-1964 Perry Mason movies I have seen, this one is my least favorite. I confess I have never liked Diana Muldaur as an actress. She always seems to be drawn to the same type of character - a hard-boiled tough woman with an undefined chip on her shoulder who looks tough but is almost impossible to in any way sympathize with. This movie is no exception, and runs true to type. The only thing that saves this movie, in my opinion, is an excellent performance by Scott Baio as Perry Mason - I actually found myself rooting for him at times, and the movie is worth seeing for him alone.

This movie would have been alright, indeed probably excellent, if the directors would have left the interviews and the concert footage separate. "Into the Void" is a great song, and I hate how it is cut off at the best part to go to an mumbling interview with Ozzy Osbourne. That should have been at the end of the film, or located in a special feature. The best part of concert DVDs is to put them on and let the music play, but "Black Sabbath: The Last Supper" is hard to put and and simply let play because the music is continually interrupted. Nevertheless, there are a few strengths to this film; the concert footage, when it does play, it excellent. Black Sabbath returns to the stage after a long hiatus without Osbourne and this film captures that well: Sabbath basically rocks the fans. The fans, of course, have a sweet advantage in the film because they are seeing the band live, of course, but also they do not have to put up with the incessant interviews that the DVD viewers are burdened with. Shame on Jeb Brien and Monica Hardiman (the directors) for doing this to the film! Also, shame on Wyatt Smith for editing the film in such a way.

This movie could have been alright, maybe even great, but the directors kept cutting between the music and the interviews is annoying. "Into the Void" is a great song, but I hate how it is cut off at the best part to go to an mumbling interview with Ozzy Osbourne. That should have been at the end of the film, or included as a bonus feature. The best part of music DVDs is to put them on and let the music play, but "Black Sabbath: The Last Stand" is frustrating to watch and and frustrating to play because the music is continually interrupted. However, there are a few strengths to the film: the concert footage, when it does play, is excellent. Black Sabbath returns to the stage after a long time without Osbourne and the film shows that they are still a very good band. The fans, of course, have a special interest in the film because they are seeing the band after years of absence, but even they should not have to put up with the incessant interviews that the casual viewers have to sit through. The directors Jeb Brien and Monica Hardiman should be ashamed of for doing this to the fans, and the producer Robert Wyatt should know why the film is such a mess

Last night, my wife and I decided to stay in, have a nice dinner, and watch this movie. Unfortunately, we were both disappointed. We're in our 40's and 50's, love romance, and are both "old school" but this movie was just not for us (it's hard to imagine how it was nominated for Oscars, etc. but I guess it was then). The cinematography was beautiful but for the most part the movie as a whole is terribly dated. Shirley Jones' character makes so many references to her horse Eurasion that we started laughing and after a while we were giggling every time she said it. Add to that the "theme song" that is played throughout the film and we couldn't wait for it to be over and get on with the evening.

I think they should seriously consider NEVER making another "epic" film again, if Noah's Ark is going to be the norm. Aside from the horrible acting and the terrible choices of the entire cast (Voight and Steenburgen undoubtedly regret the day the agreed to do this film), the time line has been completely rearranged. I also missed the part in Genesis about the animals working on the construction of the ark or the traveling salesman coming by on a paddle boat. Hello, EVERYONE else was dead except for Noah and his family according to Genesis. They stacked lumber and made plans to build the ark while Noah questioned how?? I also don't recall reading anything about the ark being floated on the river during the 40 days, or Noah wandering around glassy-eyed and dazed all the time. The script writer obviously had very little knowledge of the book of Genesis, or just didn't care. This abomination of the story completely ruins it

This frothy romantic comedy is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather distasteful. In the case of May-September attachments, doubtless what is on the mind of the elder party is either lust, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both. And the younger is most likely looking for the kind parent that she (or he) lacked as a child. These underlying agendas seem more pathetic than romantic to me now; there is also something rather predatory about them. Dick Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as well he should--at playing the elder lover in this silly story. He was, at fifty, attempting the role of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teen-ager. But young Debbie Reynolds was a knockout--pretty and saucy and full of vinegar--as a misbehaving seventeen-year-old presented as a kind of "gift" to the morally upright and honest screenwriter, as a subject for him to study. Her spirited performance wrung from me a better rating than this film would otherwise deserve. Anne Francis was cast as Powell's beautiful, but brittle fiancée, and handled her small role deftly. Some of the dialogue was quite amusing, too, so it's not a total washout. 5/10

This frothy romantic comedy is based on the kind of story that sounds like a comedy, but is really a kind of tragedy. In this kind of May-September love story, what is on the mind of the elder lover is either loneliness, or an inability to face the realities of life, or both, while the girl is most likely looking for the same love that her father had given to her as a child. These stories are not only pathetic, but to me now, there is also something rather predatory about them. William Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as well he should--at playing the elder lover in this silly comedy. He was, after all, attempting the role of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teen-ager. However, Debbie Reynolds was a revelation--bright and funny, and full of energy--as the misbehaving seventeen-year-old presented as a kind of "gift" to the more upright and serious screenwriter, as a subject for his psychological study. Her spirited performance was enough to earn a better rating than this film would otherwise deserve. Anne Francis was cast as Powell's beautiful, but brittle fiancée, and she was wasted in this role. Some of the supporting performances were good, too, so this wasn't a total washout. 5/10

I have no idea how accurate the portrayal of Flynn appears in this film but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The script is all over the place and leaves you wondering how he got from one scene to the next - you are just not given the minimum information needed to keep some continuity and understand his present situation, and it is difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motives behind some of their behaviour. Add to that a series of silly and implausible situations and you have film that comes across as one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just strange, disjointed and totally unrealistic. There are many long, boring musical sections of the film that to me are either bad direction or a bad director trying and failing to be artistic. None of the characters are even likable and the Flynn character comes across as a self serving liar, thug, thief, robber, murderer, bear fist fighter, gigolo and impostor who will do anything and step on anyone to further his own dreams, and somehow, despite all that, great opportunities just seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining nor satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even historically accurate, so why even watch it? I have no idea what the historical portrayal of Flynn is in this, but even as a work of fiction this is one of the worst movies I have ever seen. The plot is all over the place and leaves you wondering how he got from one scene to the next. You are not given all the background information you need in some scenes to understand the present situation, and it is hard to understand Flynn's and other characters' motivations behind many of their actions. Add to that a lot of silly and implausible situations and you have something that comes across as a bad fever dream that seems to make sense while you are watching, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just confusing, disjointed and illogical. There are many long and boring musical sections of the film that to me are either poor direction or just bad at storytelling and failing to be artistic. None of the characters are particularly likable and the main character comes across as a self serving liar, thief, conman, robber, murderer, bear fist fighter, gigolo and impostor who will do anything to achieve his goals and further his own interests, and somehow, despite his bad behavior, things just seem to miraculously fall into his lap. The film is neither entertaining nor educational in any way and by all accounts not even historically accurate, so why even watch it? To rub salt into the wound, the DVD was one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even a wide-screen version, it had poor color, poor contrast, telecine wobble and artifacts in many scenes on what looked like a V master that had been gathering dust for years somewhere.

This film was pure boredom from beginning to end. Ok, credit to John Boorman for raising the worldwide recognition of events in Bosnia, but that's all he achieved. About 10 minutes into the film I thought, "Oh, here we go again", and I could have told you exactly what was going to happen for the next 80 minutes or so. Patricia Arquette was out of her depth in such a role, and her performance was wooden and unconvincing. When you've been saddled with a predictable and conventional script, maybe boredom set in, and as such reflected on her performance. A lot of the film was just plain laughable. In one scene, we see an elderly man get shot, and he is prostrate on the ground. In the next scene, he is sprinting across the room, obviously trying to break the world 100m record! No wait, he's just trying to run away from Boorman!!. If you find it hard to sleep sometimes, then play Beyond the Border on your VCR and you'll be out in no time. It's rarely that I criticize a film as heavily as this, but in this case it was necessary.

Pointless and pretty silly film that is just basically a compilation of clips from horror, science fiction and suspense films. There are unnecessary shots to an audience watching the clips and Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen are among audience members who turn to the camera and explain why we love horror films. Not a bad idea but all the explanations are obvious ("movie horror helps us deal with real horror", "you are at the mercy of the filmmaker in a theatre") and pretty trite. Also the clips are shown very quickly and the changes are kind of jarring. And, shown out of context, these bits aren't very scary at all. And it's REAL short--I saw it in a theatre back in 1984 and was outraged that I paid $5.00 for an 84 minute movie! Still, it is reasonably well-edited and Allen and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. For people who have an interest in knowing more about terror this might be fun and interesting. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be bored silly. Good idea, bad execution (no pun intended). I give it a 3.

Pointless. A silly film that seems to be a mix of several different horror, science fiction and comedy films. There are unnecessary shots of an audience in the theatre and Donald Pleasance and Nancy Allen play two audience members who talk to the camera and explain why we hate horror movies. Not a bad idea but all the explanations are obvious ("movie horror doesn't deal with real horror", "we're at the mercy of the people in the theatre") and not very funny. The horror scenes are shown very slowly and the changes are abrupt and and sudden. And, shown so slowly, the scary bits are not very scary. And finally, it's REAL long. I saw it in a theatre back in 1984 and was annoyed that I paid $5.00 for an 84-minute film. On the plus side it's reasonably well-edited and Allen and Pleasance seem to be enjoying themselves. For people who have an interest in comedy more than terror this film might be more interesting. But if you're a horror fan (like me) you'll probably be bored silly. Good actors, bad film (no pun intended). I give it a 3.

Wow, I'm going to have to watch Trollrolls and Anus Plague again, just to see if it's possible to get past the hamfistedly clichéd dialogue. I was so tortured that taking a plane from from Germany to the DR Congo might well be preferable to sitting through this. The only remotely realism it manages to achieve is in its depiction of the plague-stricken natives, who turn to a simple, dumb, collective prayer which does nothing until the übermenschlich, linen-clad missionary manages to convince the village elder, with a direct appeal to Yahweh, to provide a urine sample which the missionary's in-house microbi team can then get to work on to save the hapless natives. This movie sucks.

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

This film, which purports to be murder mystery, unfortunately does the opposite of just that. Raymond Massey plays a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his disguises, which put him in a farm laborer's garb, in the grand mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What remains a mystery to me is why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If, in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to be in love with Holmes, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. Despite setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is seen nor heard from for the remainder of the picture. The cause of the death of the Stoner and the disappearance of the Stoner's daughter is also a mystery, turning what could have been an interesting murder mystery into a confusing mess.. I could't tell that it was a Sherlock Holmes film, the musical renderings of the Sherlock Holmes theme notwithstanding. Athole performs competently as Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though it takes some getting used to. Nigel Bruce is not my cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a quality that would be put to good use as the villainous Dr. Moriarty in two later films, 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With the film's slow pace and unsteady editing, it's surprising that the story's plot is as coherent as it is. It's continuity is well maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main criticism of the film, as mentally filling some of the jump cuts in the film proved to be a real pain in the aspic

Put simply, this mini-series was terrible. Let me count the ways. 1. Absurd plotting. 2. Over-acting. 3. Scattershot approach to characters. 4. Annoying narration. 5. Inability to create viewer interest. This film can't even pass the "Soap Opera for Dummies" test. I'm sorry I have not read this award-winning novel, so I am judging it only as a film, but it really stinks. Imagine going to a party where they show you dozens of appetizers. You look at the wide variety and want to taste them, but suddenly they are withdrawn, and you wonder where they went. That's like this film, with way too many characters introduced and never drawn out. There are enough stories and characters in this film to create a 20 episode series, yet we are given less than four hours to digest it all. There are more facial expressions and reaction shots of Ed Harris than you'll find on 10,000 monkeys. The pace is extraordinarily slow. Dennis Farina and Helen Hunt are so far over-the-top that their characters are not believable. Joanne Woodward's character is one-dimensional. The persistent river metaphor becomes trite. And, probably the most absurd part of the film--the cat. This evil and vengeful cat who follows the hero around to scratch him and his seat covers--well, come on now---it's not even good Stephen King! Probably the most interesting character in the film, and one who is not drawn well, is John Voss, the disturbed boy whose final act of desperation accounts for the only plot device that works in this film. Just about everyone in this film is unbelievable. To sum up, there's little here to inspire. The drama is poor melodrama. It's just a terrible effort.

Put simply, this mini-series is terrible. Let me count the ways: 1. Terrible plotting. 2. Over-the-top acting. 3. Lack of character development. 4. Annoying narration. 5. Inability to create viewer interest. This film is really more of a "Soap Opera for Dummies" film. I'm sorry I have not read this award-winning novel, so I am judging it only as a film, but it really is like going to a fancy dinner party where they show you all the appetizers. You stare at them wide-eyed, wanting to taste them, but suddenly they are withdrawn, and you wonder what went wrong. In this film, there are too many characters and too long drawn out. There are enough stories and characters in this film to fill a 10-hour series, yet we are given less than two hours to digest it all. There are more close-ups and reaction shots of Ed Harris than you'll see on screen in 1000 years. The pacing is too slow and dragging. Dennis Farina and Helen Hunt are both too over-the-top in their performances to be believable. Edward Woodward's character is one-dimensional. The use of the river metaphor is trite. And, probably the most annoying part of the film--the narration by the young and emotionallyumbling Ed Harris who has to turn around and scratch him and his seat again--oh, come on now---he's not even good at narrating. The only interesting character in the film, and one who is not drawn well, is Ed Harris, the emotionally disturbed boy whose final act of bravery accounts for the only plot device that works in this film. Just about everyone in this film is unbelievable. To sum up, there is little here to recommend. The drama is a mess, and the acting is a terrible effort

He, like most involved, played the 007 role with kind hearts, and while the general response has been largely negative, for those who thought he was faking it, he was living it!

My guess is that the producers of this low-budget space/horror film wanted a serious movie but the director had his heart set on a parody. So...this is what we get. Set in an abandoned spaceship 1000 years in the future and peopled with characters and props right out of the 90's. The set is some industrial complex, maybe an oil tanker, whatever. They use is AS IS so the controls consist racks of old TV equipment. One location is obviously the employees lunchroom and sports an old TV and VCR as well as a water cooler with plastic demijohn. Tiny Lister and Coolio get the best lines, arguing throughout the story. The dialog is packed with terms that are pretty dated even now ("A-OK, Daddy-O") but then maybe the 30th century is very retro? When the captain declares the ships cargo is a load of coffins from "The Transylvania Station" you know this is all a put-on. Its a bit of Alien, part JasonX, shameless rip-off of all the best sci-fi and horror titles. At one point Casper VanDien even tells his pilot to "make it so" with a straight face. This film would have been better if they had just let everyone run with the satire but they keep attempting to make the story serious....maybe the backers were on the set that day. Anyway, not a bad boredom killer if you aren't too picky. FX are as good as the sets are bad.

My guess is that the producers of this low-budget space/horror film wanted a serious movie but the director had his heart set on a satirical film--this is what you get. Set on an abandoned spaceship, 100 years in the future, it's filled with sets and props straight out of the past. The first scene is set in some industrial complex, where an oil tanker is parked. They use a Lexus IS and the walls consist racks of old TV equipment. One location is called an employees' lounge and sports an old TV and VCR as well as a water cooler and a demijohn. Dave Lister and Coolio get the best lines, sprinkled throughout the story. The crew members use slang terms that I don't even know ("A-List, Daddy-O") but who in the 30th century is this retro? When the captain of the spaceship is trying to get a phone signal to the International Space Station, you know this is not a straight-on. Its a parody of Alien, part JasonX, and a rip-off of all the other sci-fi and horror movies. At one point, the captain of the ship tells his pilot to "tell it so" with a straight face. This movie would have been great if they had just let it run with the satire but they keep attempting to make the story serious--maybe the backers had a deadline set that day. It's not a bad movie, if you're not too picky. They are as good as the others are bad.

Though a fan of shock and gore, I found this movie disappointing to say the very least. The effects and puppet work were impressive, yes, and the humor was well-timed, but... something was missing. See, the first act of the film is spent establishing nuances of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is delivered within minutes of the first title cards. As for the narration and many of the flashbacks: needless. The pacing during the second act was tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then vomiting, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying something snappy or rude. All the while, the schlock is punctuated with brief scenes of Jack discussing his rage problems with a therapist. (Definitely the entertaining scenes in the film -- excellent dialog worth plenty of laughs.) Then, without warning, Jack decides to kill a few monsters. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has loads of potential but is purposeless and plods on without conflict or adequate resolution. Hopefully, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack Goes to Hell or Jack vs. Ash go into production.

Though a fan of shock and gore, I found this film disappointing to say the very least. The blood and gore were there, sure, and the violence was well-executed. However, something was missing. First, the first act of the film is mostly establishing shots of Jack Brooks' character, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is delivered within minutes of the opening title cards. Also, the therapist and his series of flashbacks: unnecessary. The pacing of the second act was slow. Most of it is taken up of scenes of Brooks eating, then sleeping, then eating some more, then flailing his arms and killing something. The pacing is slow and and predictable. The third act opens with a scene of Jack discussing his anger issues with a therapist. Given the violence established earlier in the film, the dialog feels out of place. Then, of course, he decides to kill a few people. And then it's over. All in all, as a throwback to 1980s horror movies, Jack Brooks: Serial Killer has a lot of potential but ultimately fallsanders and plods on without providing an adequate resolution. For a better, more satisfying horror film of this era, try out Evilam, Hellraiser , or Ash Williams..

But I was dumb that day, because I did something I should have never done. I rented a "Straight To Video Independent Horror Film" Walking out with my much better rentals, I went home, popped Dark Harvest in the DVD player and it began. I figured I would watch the trailer after the film was done (BAD IDEA) but went ahead and watched it anyway. NOW to the review.*POSSIBLE SPOILERS* First off, the acting by the "kids" sucks, and the scene when the 2 (main characters) are talking, the lighting sucks, and the buildings even look fake! Now they go to this house, where Sean Connel's (I think he's the main character, I don't care) relatives lived there. All of a sudden one by one, they all start getting killed by...(gasp) A KILLER SCARECROW!!!! AHHH!!!!! Save yourself some time, I'm telling you this movie sucks. if you need to pass an hour and a half, look at the wall, because looking at the wall is A+ fun compared to this disaster. It is quite funny though. Overall Grade: F If there was anything lower **F-** Than I would give it that.

NOW THE MOV REVIEW.*POSSIBLE SPOILERS* First off, the acting is terrible, the plot sucks, and the scene when the 2 (main characters) are driving, the lighting sucks, and it doesn't look real. Now they go to the house, and the Connel's (I think he's the main character, I don't care) family are there. All of a sudden one by one, and they are getting killed by (gasp) A COMPUTERIZED SCARECROW!!!!!!)!!. The scarecrow is obviously the star of the movie, and the scene where the scarecrow is computerized looks so fake it's hilarious. It makes creepy noises and everything! And then at the end...they show the scarecrow with a gun (which is red for Pete's sake and looks like it was bought at a local family dollar) and it shoots thenel, and then.....(gulp) IT BLOWS UP!!!!!!)!!. for some reason. I'm telling you this movie sucks, if you want to waste an hour and a half, then watch this movie, but Shaun of the Dead is A LOT fun compared to this disaster. It's quite funny though, I guess. Grade: F If there was a grade lower than F, Than I would give it that.

This movie is based on the series Street Fighter II (video game). It is placed in an other setting than Streetfighter II's Japan. This movie is all about Ryu who is the main character and Chun Li who is recognized as the "Fly Birdie". There are not any other characters used from the video game (that i could discover). The fighting scenes were okay but not that spectacular. And there were not many of them either. The story is boring! Isn't that the main of of Streetfighter II in the fighting game? The video game is far superior to this movie. It tries to be more than it can be! The use of the "Hada Power" and other mystical elemnents have nothing to do with skills the characters have in the video game! And in this case that is a bad thing! The story is so boring that you don't really care what is happening. The action is slowed down considerably! Why? Why not use on the other characters from the video game? Surely they are more interesting than the ones in this story? The main attraction of the video game is the characters with different styles and skills. In this movie it is all about Ryu and Chun Li and that is boring!
